# Resistance Scaling in Single-Walled Carbon Nanotube Devices

This study experimentally investigates how electrical resistance scales in individual single-walled carbon nanotube devices, examining channel lengths that span four orders of magnitude on the same sample. By probing such a wide range of length scales within a single device, the research provides a comprehensive picture of the transport behavior while eliminating the sample-to-sample variability that often complicates comparisons across different devices.

A central quantity extracted from these measurements is the electron mean free path, which is determined from the linear scaling of resistance with channel length measured at various temperatures. In the diffusive regime, resistance increases linearly with the length of the conducting channel, and the slope of this relationship allows the mean free path to be quantified as a function of temperature.

The temperature dependence of the mean free path reveals two distinct scattering regimes. At low temperatures, the mean free path is governed primarily by impurity scattering, reflecting the influence of static defects and disorder within the nanotube. In contrast, at high temperatures the mean free path decreases with rising temperature, a behavior attributable to electron-phonon scattering, whereby thermally excited lattice vibrations increasingly limit electron transport.

Notably, the researchers experimentally confirmed an unusually long electron mean free path at room temperature. This finding underscores the exceptional transport properties of single-walled carbon nanotubes and highlights their potential for applications in high-performance nanoscale electronic devices, where minimizing scattering is critical.

Finally, the study observes that resistance increases exponentially at extremely long length scales. This exponential growth, which departs from the simple linear scaling characteristic of diffusive transport, indicates the presence of anomalous localization effects. Such behavior points to the quantum-mechanical interference of electron waves in the presence of disorder, revealing the rich and complex nature of charge transport in these one-dimensional systems.

# Resistance Scaling in Single-Walled Carbon Nanotube Devices

## Introduction

Single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWNTs) have long been recognized as exceptional electronic materials, distinguished by their remarkable ability to conduct electrons over extraordinarily long distances with minimal scattering. Understanding how electrical resistance scales with channel length is fundamental to both the basic physics of these one-dimensional conductors and their potential applications in next-generation electronic devices. To systematically investigate this behavior, researchers undertook a comprehensive experimental study measuring individual carbon nanotube samples across an exceptionally wide range of channel lengths.

## Experimental Approach

The study examined nanotube devices with channel lengths spanning four orders of magnitude, from the shortest to the longest configurations, enabling an unprecedented view of transport behavior across dramatically different length regimes. For each sample, resistance measurements were performed at various temperatures to disentangle the different physical mechanisms governing charge transport. By analyzing how resistance scaled linearly with increasing channel length, the researchers were able to extract the electron mean free path—the average distance an electron travels before undergoing a scattering event—at each temperature investigated.

## Key Findings

The results confirmed that single-walled carbon nanotubes possess an unusually long mean free path at room temperature, underscoring their status as near-ballistic conductors. The temperature dependence of the mean free path revealed two distinct scattering regimes. At high temperatures, transport was limited primarily by electron-phonon scattering, as thermally excited lattice vibrations increasingly impeded electron motion. In contrast, at low temperatures, where phonon activity was suppressed, the mean free path became limited by impurity scattering arising from defects and disorder within the nanotube structure.

## Anomalous Localization Effects

Beyond confirming the expected scattering physics, the study uncovered a striking anomaly at extremely long length scales. Rather than continuing to increase linearly, the resistance began to rise exponentially as the channel length grew very large. This exponential dependence is a hallmark of localization effects, in which quantum interference and disorder conspire to trap electrons and dramatically suppress conduction. The observation of such anomalous behavior in these long-channel devices highlights the subtle interplay between the intrinsically long mean free path of carbon nanotubes and the localization phenomena that emerge when transport is probed over sufficiently large distances.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these findings provide a detailed picture of resistance scaling in single-walled carbon nanotubes, spanning from the near-ballistic regime at short lengths to the localized regime at extreme lengths. The work not only quantifies the temperature-dependent mean free path and identifies the dominant scattering mechanisms, but also reveals unexpected localization effects that deepen our understanding of one-dimensional electronic transport in these remarkable materials.

# The Exponentially Changing World

We live in an era defined by exponential change. Unlike the steady, linear progress that characterized much of human history, the modern world advances at a pace that doubles, redoubles, and accelerates beyond our intuitive grasp. Understanding this phenomenon—the exponentially expanding frontier of technology, information, and connection—is essential for navigating the future.

## Understanding Exponential Growth

The human mind naturally thinks in linear terms. When we imagine progress, we picture a gentle, predictable slope. Exponential growth, however, behaves differently. It starts slowly, almost imperceptibly, and then surges upward with startling speed. The classic example is the story of the chessboard, where a single grain of rice placed on the first square, doubled on each subsequent square, eventually amounts to more rice than exists on Earth.

This is why exponential trends so often catch us by surprise. What seems insignificant today can transform entire industries tomorrow.

## The Forces Driving Exponential Progress

Several domains are being reshaped exponentially:

- **Computing power** has famously doubled roughly every two years, following Moore's Law.
- **Data generation** grows relentlessly as billions of devices constantly record and transmit information.
- **Artificial intelligence** improves at a rate that compounds upon its own advancements.
- **Global connectivity** expands as more people join digital networks each day.

Each of these areas feeds the others, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of acceleration.

## Living in an Exponential Age

The challenge—and opportunity—lies in adapting our expectations. Institutions, education systems, and individuals accustomed to gradual change must learn to anticipate rapid, transformative shifts. Those who recognize the exponential nature of progress can prepare, innovate, and thrive, while those who cling to linear thinking may find themselves left behind.

The exponentially evolving landscape demands both caution and curiosity. It reminds us that the future arrives faster than we expect, and that today's small beginnings may become tomorrow's overwhelming realities.

# Abstract

We report systematic measurements of electrical resistance as a function of channel length in single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) field-effect transistors, providing direct insight into charge transport mechanisms and the electron mean free path in these quasi-one-dimensional conductors. Using a series of individually contacted metallic and semiconducting SWCNTs with channel lengths ranging from 100 nm to 5 μm, we extract the length-dependent resistance under controlled gate bias and temperature conditions. Our data reveal a clear transition from ballistic to diffusive transport as the channel length exceeds the electron mean free path. In the short-channel regime, the resistance approaches the quantum limit of h/4e² (~6.5 kΩ), consistent with ballistic conduction through the four parallel channels of a SWCNT. For longer channels, resistance increases linearly with length, from which we extract a room-temperature mean free path of approximately 1 μm for high-quality metallic tubes—significantly longer than in conventional semiconductors. Temperature-dependent measurements indicate that acoustic phonon scattering dominates the mean free path at room temperature, while optical and zone-boundary phonon scattering become relevant at high bias. These results quantitatively separate the contact resistance from the intrinsic channel resistance and establish scaling relationships essential for evaluating the potential of SWCNTs in nanoscale electronic interconnects and devices. Our findings underscore the exceptional low-scattering transport properties of carbon nanotubes and provide benchmark parameters for modeling electron dynamics in one-dimensional systems.

# Electronic Transport in Carbon Nanotubes: Scattering Mechanisms and Localization

## Abstract

Charge transport in carbon nanotubes (CNTs) is governed by an interplay of scattering mechanisms that determine the mean free path and, ultimately, the conductance regime. In high-quality single-walled nanotubes, the intrinsic mean free path can reach several micrometers, enabling quasi-ballistic transport in which electrons traverse the channel with minimal backscattering. This behavior arises from the reduced phase space for scattering in a one-dimensional system and the suppression of backscattering by the symmetry of the graphene-derived band structure.

At low temperatures and bias, transport is often limited by **impurity and defect scattering**, including charged impurities in the substrate, structural defects, and adsorbed molecules. These static scatterers introduce elastic backscattering that shortens the mean free path and can produce conductance fluctuations sensitive to the local disorder configuration. As **temperature or bias increases**, **electron-phonon scattering** becomes dominant. Coupling to acoustic phonons yields a temperature-dependent resistance in the low-bias regime, while high-energy optical and zone-boundary phonons impose a saturation of the current at high bias, setting a characteristic short mean free path (~10–15 nm) once carriers acquire sufficient energy to emit optical phonons.

When elastic scattering is strong and phase coherence is maintained, quantum interference of backscattered electron waves can drive the system toward **weak and strong localization**. In the one-dimensional limit, states become localized on a length scale set by the elastic mean free path and the number of conducting channels, leading to an exponential suppression of conductance with length and characteristic temperature-dependent transport. The relative importance of these mechanisms depends on tube diameter, chirality, defect density, temperature, and applied bias, making CNTs a rich platform for exploring low-dimensional quantum transport.

# Abstract

The electrical transport properties of single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWNTs) are critically dependent on channel length, yet systematic investigations spanning a wide dimensional range within individual nanotubes remain limited. Here, we present an experimental study of resistance scaling in individual metallic and semiconducting SWNTs across channel lengths ranging from tens of nanometers to hundreds of micrometers, encompassing four orders of magnitude. Using a multi-electrode contact architecture fabricated on individual chirality-characterized nanotubes, we performed length-dependent, four-probe resistance measurements that decouple intrinsic channel resistance from contact contributions. Our results reveal three distinct transport regimes governed by the interplay between channel length and characteristic scattering lengths. In the short-channel limit, transport approaches the ballistic regime, with resistance approaching the quantum limit of h/4e² and exhibiting weak length dependence. At intermediate lengths, resistance scales quasi-linearly, consistent with quasi-ballistic transport dominated by acoustic phonon scattering and a corresponding mean free path on the order of one micrometer. In the long-channel regime, we observe a transition to diffusive transport, with resistance increasing superlinearly due to the combined effects of optical phonon and defect scattering. Temperature-dependent measurements further elucidate the relative contributions of elastic and inelastic scattering mechanisms across these regimes. By probing multiple length scales within the same nanotube, we eliminate sample-to-sample variability and extract intrinsic scattering parameters with high fidelity. These findings provide a unified framework for understanding charge transport in one-dimensional carbon nanostructures and offer quantitative design guidelines for the integration of SWNTs into nanoscale interconnects and field-effect devices.

# Temperature-Dependent Mean Free Path Measurements in Carbon Nanotube Devices: Long Room-Temperature Transport and Anomalous Localization

## Abstract

We report systematic measurements of the electron mean free path in individual single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) field-effect devices as a function of temperature spanning 4 K to 300 K. Using a combination of length-dependent resistance analysis and four-probe transport spectroscopy on suspended and substrate-supported nanotubes, we extract the intrinsic mean free path while decoupling contributions from acoustic phonon scattering, optical/zone-boundary phonon emission, and static disorder. At room temperature, we observe a remarkably long mean free path exceeding 1 μm in high-quality metallic tubes, consistent with weak acoustic-phonon-limited backscattering and confirming the near-ballistic nature of low-bias transport in defect-free SWCNTs. The mean free path exhibits an approximately inverse dependence on temperature ($\ell \propto T^{-1}$) in the intermediate regime, in agreement with a deformation-potential model of acoustic phonon scattering.

Contrary to the expectation of monotonically increasing coherence and conductance at low temperatures, a subset of devices displays **anomalous localization behavior**: as temperature decreases below approximately 20 K, the resistance rises sharply and the effective mean free path collapses, accompanied by a transition from metallic to insulating-like temperature dependence. This localization is characterized by reproducible conductance fluctuations and a saturation of the phase coherence length, indicating that quantum interference from residual disorder dominates transport once thermal dephasing is suppressed. We find that the onset temperature and strength of localization correlate with contact quality and substrate-induced potential fluctuations rather than intrinsic defect density, suggesting an extrinsic origin for the anomalous low-temperature regime. Weak-localization magnetoresistance measurements further support a picture of crossover from quasi-ballistic, phonon-limited transport at high temperature to a disorder-dominated, phase-coherent regime at cryogenic temperatures.

These results reconcile the coexistence of micron-scale room-temperature mean free paths with low-temperature localization, and highlight the critical role of environmental disorder in determining the temperature-dependent transport of nanotube devices. Our findings have direct implications for the design of nanotube-based interconnects and coherent quantum devices, where operating temperature strongly modulates the balance between phonon scattering and quantum interference.

---

*Keywords:* carbon nanotubes, mean free path, electron–phonon scattering, quantum localization, ballistic transport, phase coherence

We report a systematic investigation of electronic transport in carbon nanotubes spanning channel lengths across four orders of magnitude, all measured on a single sample to eliminate device-to-device variability. By analyzing the linear scaling of resistance with channel length at multiple temperatures, we extracted the temperature-dependent mean free path governing charge carrier transport. Notably, at very long channel lengths, we observed a crossover to exponential growth in resistance, indicating a transition in the dominant transport mechanism. These results provide a comprehensive, self-consistent picture of length- and temperature-dependent transport in nanotube channels and offer insight into the interplay between scattering processes across disparate length scales.
